title: Best Score Hopping At Most K
statement:
A row of tiles is described by nums. You stand on tile 0 and want to reach the last tile. From tile i you may hop to any tile i + 1 through i + k, as long as it exists.

Your score is the sum of nums over every tile you stand on, including the first and the last. Tiles can be negative. Return the largest score you can finish with.

examples.why: Take 0 → 2 → 3 → 5: 2 − 1 + 6 + 1 = 8. Hopping to the nearest positive tile is not possible from 0, so you pick the smaller loss −1 over −4.
With k = 1 every tile is visited: 5 − 3 + 3 = 5.
One hop straight to the end skips every negative tile. The last tile is always counted.

hints: Let best[i] be the largest score that ends standing on tile i. How does best[i] depend on earlier tiles?
best[i] = nums[i] + max(best[i − k], …, best[i − 1]). Computing that maximum by scanning is O(k) per tile. The window of candidates slides one step each time.
Keep a deque of indexes whose best values are decreasing. Drop indexes from the front once they fall out of the window, and drop smaller values from the back before pushing i.

explain.intuition:
The best way to arrive at tile i is to come from whichever of the previous k tiles had the highest score so far. So best[i] = nums[i] + max(best[i − k .. i − 1]). That is a sliding-window maximum, and greedy shortcuts like "hop to the next non-negative tile" fail because sometimes every reachable tile is negative and you must pick the least bad one.

A monotonic deque answers each window maximum in O(1) on average. It holds indexes whose best values decrease from front to back. A new index makes every smaller value behind it useless forever: it is newer, so it stays in the window longer, and it is at least as good. So pop those, push the new one, and the front is always the window's maximum.
steps: Set best[0] = nums[0] and put index 0 in the deque.
For each i from 1: pop the front while it is older than i − k.
Pop the back while its best is ≤ best[i], then push i.
pitfalls: Greedily hopping to the nearest non-negative tile, or the largest tile in reach. A larger tile now can strand you in front of worse tiles later.
Evicting by value instead of by index. The deque must store indexes so you know when one leaves the window.
Off-by-one on the window: tile i − k is still reachable, tile i − k − 1 is not.

solutions.title: Plain DP over the window
solutions.idea: For every tile, scan the previous k scores for the maximum.

solutions.title: Max-heap with lazy removal
solutions.idea: Keep (score, index) pairs in a max-heap and discard the top while its index is outside the window.

solutions.title: DP with a monotonic deque
solutions.idea: The deque keeps window indexes with decreasing scores, so its front is always the best tile to hop from.

followups: Return the actual list of tiles you stood on, not just the score.
Hops may now be between a and b tiles long (a > 1). How does the window change?
